body: The report shows active diplomacy but no convergence, so markets are unlikely to price a settlement soon. European defence stocks are the most headline-sensitive, and any sign of a breakthrough would test their rally. A credible peace path would eventually weigh on European gas prices and diesel cracks, where Russian refining and product exports have been a supply risk, and could support the euro. For oil, the Middle East remains the bigger driver, so Ukraine headlines are a secondary factor for crude itself. Washington has put Ukraine’s NATO membership on the table as a bargaining chip, but Moscow wants the opposite and Berlin isn’t on board, so a deal still looks distant. US envoys have floated the idea of NATO membership for Ukraine in exchange for Kyiv ceding territory to Russia, a proposal that would break with long-standing US policy and run directly against Moscow’s demands, The Wall Street Journal (gated) reported. According to people familiar with the talks cited by the Journal, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff have raised the idea in several conversations with European officials in recent months. Most recently it came up with President Volodymyr Zelensky and European national security advisers at a meeting in Dublin last week. It was also raised in at least one meeting in the United Arab Emirates involving Ukrainian, European and Russian negotiators. The US has put two scenarios on the table, the report said. The first would see Ukraine give up the part of the Donbas region it still controls in return for full NATO membership. The second would freeze the conflict along the current front line, leaving some of the Donbas in Ukrainian hands, with security guarantees provided through a treaty with the US and possibly European allies. A US official said many ideas are under discussion and that both Ukraine and Russia would have to agree to any final deal. It is unclear how seriously the idea is being pursued, or whether President Donald Trump has changed his view. He ruled out Ukrainian NATO membership early last year as unacceptable to Russia. Zelensky confirmed the question had been raised, recounting that the Americans asked, “What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?” He has said repeatedly that Ukraine will not give up its land, and that any deal would need approval from the Ukrainian people. Moscow’s position points the other way. In a non-paper seen by the Journal, Russian negotiators demanded that Ukraine remove its NATO aspirations from its constitution, that the alliance commit not to station troops or equipment in Ukraine, and that Western arms deliveries stop. They also called for NATO to roll back military infrastructure in Eastern Europe to 1997 levels. European negotiators described the demands as maximalist opening bids. Divisions within NATO add a further hurdle, since the alliance can only expand by consensus. French President Emmanuel Macron said after talks in Berlin on Thursday that it was time to discuss Ukraine’s membership. German officials were unwilling to pursue it, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz has told aides he does not expect Ukraine to join in his lifetime. Kushner said separately that Russia had become comfortable with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine. For markets, the report is a reminder that peace talks are active but far from a deal. Any credible move toward a settlement would be watched closely in European defence stocks, European gas prices and the euro, and in oil product markets, where Russian refining and export flows have been a source of supply risk. Bitcoin fell to around $61,600 on Thursday, its lowest level since early July. The move came as a 1,000-point drop in the Dow and fresh talk of tighter Federal Reserve policy pushed investors out of riskier assets. The token was down a little over 2% on the day by early evening in New York, leaving it within reach of the $60,000 mark and roughly half its record high. The selling tracked Wall Street closely. body: The disclosure adds to political pressure for tighter China chip rules, a risk for Nvidia and AMD’s China revenue at a time when AI and semiconductor shares are already being sold hard across Asia. Nvidia saying it has stopped H200 shipments limits the near-term earnings hit, but any formal tightening would also weigh on Chinese AI developers’ access to computing power. Hong Kong-listed Tencent, Alibaba and Baidu are the most exposed names on the Chinese side. The story also keeps Washington’s broader export-control push in focus, including reported plans to curb advanced chip exports to parts of Southeast Asia. Washington’s own licensing data show it cleared hundreds of thousands of AI chips for Chinese firms, including military-listed ones, handing China hawks fresh ammunition just as Nvidia says it has stopped shipping. The US Commerce Department approved shipments of about 880,000 advanced AI chips made by Nvidia and AMD to Chinese companies between December 2025 and May 2026, according to licensing data released on Thursday by the House Foreign Affairs Committee. The approvals covered Nvidia’s H200 and AMD’s equivalent MI325X. They included 150,000 chips for Tencent, 75,000 for Alibaba, 43,000 for Baidu and 4,000 for BYD. All four companies appear on the Pentagon’s list of alleged Chinese military-backed firms, and together they account for just over 30% of the approved total. Companies had sought permission to ship more than 3.4 million chips over the period, so roughly a quarter of requested volumes were approved. It is not clear how many of the approvals turned into actual deliveries. Nvidia said the licences came with strict conditions and limited volumes and that “we have since stopped shipping H200s to China.” AMD said it complies with US export control laws. Reuters reported in May that about 10 Chinese companies had been cleared to buy the H200 but no deliveries had been made. A Commerce official later told the committee that shipments had begun but there had been very few. The Commerce Department said its H200 licensing follows a January 2026 rule that adds significant national security requirements for applicants, allowing case-by-case review rather than a presumption of denial. Critics are unconvinced. A former US official who specialises in US-China technology policy called the share going to military-listed firms astonishing and questioned whether Commerce had carried out a serious security review. The release is unusual. Committee Chair Brian Mast described it as the most detailed public disclosure since the Export Control Reform Act of 2018 expanded Commerce’s powers over sensitive technology exports. It comes as the Trump administration faces closer scrutiny of its China chip policy following reports involving former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang and an alleged Chinese spy, which have revived calls in Washington for a tougher stance. The policy backdrop has swung sharply. The Biden administration restricted Chinese access to advanced AI chips over concerns they would strengthen China’s military and erode the US lead in AI. President Trump reversed course in December 2025, allowing Nvidia to ship the H200 to China. With pressure building on both sides of the political divide, investors will watch for any move to tighten licensing again. That would weigh on chipmakers’ China revenue and on Chinese tech firms’ access to advanced computing. Your market education doesn't end here. In 2024, the U.S. bought all but 0.01% of Canada’s natural gas exports. Ottawa now wants 55% of those exports to go to other countries by the mid-2030s, and Germany’s state-owned Uniper has signed a 20-year deal for liquefied natural gas from a planned British Columbia terminal. Prime Minister Mark Carney has fast-tracked a state-backed pipeline to carry 1 million barrels a day of Alberta crude to the Pacific coast for Asian buyers, and Alberta has cut royalties on new oil sands projects to 2% to double output by 2035. Carney took that strategy to Shenzhen this week for the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, which opened on Wednesday with leaders and business executives from 21 member economies. He met Chinese President Xi Jinping on Tuesday and spoke briefly with U.S. President Donald Trump on the sidelines on Wednesday. Afterward, Carney’s office said the two had discussed “the work underway to reach a mutually beneficial trade agreement.” Trump is set to hold a historic trilateral meeting with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday, where the White House says he will discuss reducing nuclear weapons. The brief meeting with Trump is unlikely to thaw trade tensions between the two neighbours or change Canada’s new energy trajectory. Trump has targeted Canada with sweeping tariffs and public criticism throughout his second term, turning a trade dispute into a broader diplomatic fight. In August, Trump imposed 50% tariffs on roughly US$20 billion worth of Canadian goods, with 50% tariffs on Canadian cars, auto parts and steel set to take effect on January 1, 2027. Carney has answered with retaliatory tariffs while pursuing trade deals elsewhere, including with China. China agreed to remove or reduce tariffs on about $400 million in additional Canadian exports, including frozen pork and seafood. Canada extended existing tariff exemptions on certain Chinese steel and aluminum products for another two years and added relief for 32 more steel and aluminum items in short supply domestically. The two leaders also discussed cooperation in oil and gas, and Canadian exports to China rose almost 40% in the first nine months of the year. Canada is also working to attract the capital it needs to build energy infrastructure and reduce its reliance on the U.S. market. Last week, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith’s government introduced a 10-year preferential royalty framework for new oil sands developments and expansions. Projects that add at least 5,000 barrels per day will pay a 2% gross revenue royalty for their first five years of production, rising by one percentage point a year to 6% in years nine and ten. The framework is designed to help the province double output to 8 million barrels per day by 2035. Alberta estimates that reaching that target could generate about 205 billion Canadian dollars in additional government revenue by 2040 and more than $1.3 trillion by 2060. Smith said in March that Asian and Middle Eastern investors, including sovereign wealth funds, were willing to take 15% to 30% stakes in a new West Coast pipeline. The United States remains by far the biggest buyer of Canadian energy, taking 90.8% of Canada’s hydrocarbon exports by volume through decades of integrated cross-border pipelines and power grids. Oil majors are expanding exploration across South America, Africa and Asia, seeking to replicate Guyana’s success as geopolitical disruptions reinforce the importance of new supplies. Exxon announced this week that total oil production in Guyana had topped 1 million barrels. Guyana’s transformation into a formidable oil power is now motivating other oil majors to seek opportunities to replicate Exxon’s story. It is quite easy to see why. Exxon, along with its partners Hess Corp. and CNOOC, spent billions on developing the Stabroek Block offshore the tiny South American country. The investment paid off with a string of discoveries opening up resources estimated at over 11 billion barrels of crude. With this year’s massive supply disruption because of the war between the United States and Israel, and Iran, Guyana turned into an even bigger star in Exxon’s portfolio, boosting profits. The Financial Times noted in a report this week that Exxon’s Guyana bet, which began back in 1999, when the company acquired the Stabroek Block, went against the mainstream in the industry. Active exploration offshore Guyana began in the late 2000s, and in 2015, Exxon, Hess, and CNOOC struck their first oil. But 2015 was also the year of the Paris Agreement and what many saw as a turning tide moving away from oil and gas and into alternative, low-carbon energy. Related: 5 Oil and Gas Stocks That Crushed Third-Quarter Earnings Estimates Over the past decade, the green investment movement gathered momentum, prompting oil and gas companies to make investor reward a top priority, pushing exploration and growth to the back seat. Not Exxon, however. Exxon was spending billions in Guyana and drilling for more oil when pretty much every forecasting outlet was saying peak oil demand was nigh. The forecasts have yet to come true, while this year the world got a stark reminder of just how vital crude oil and natural gas are for the proper functioning of any economy, including the greenest--the European Union’s oil and gas imports did not slump as a result of the Middle East disruption. They moved slightly lower while soaring in value because of the oil and gas price shock. “It was the textbook definition of right place, right time. It became one of the crown jewels of ExxonMobil’s repositioning, demonstrating that the company could still deliver enormous resource additions and highly competitive barrels,” Rystad Energy analyst Schreiner Parker told the Financial Times. Yet there is more to the story than just the right place and right time. It was the willingness to risk billions in investment on oil when everyone was saying oil was on its way out--and do it fast, no less. “What is particularly remarkable is the speed of development: going from first oil in 2019 to more than 1mn barrels per day in just seven years, a feat seemingly only doable by ExxonMobil. Guyana has gone from an exploration success to one of the most important pillars of ExxonMobil’s global upstream growth strategy,” Rystad’s Parker also told the FT. summary: The core inflation figure — which strips out prices of food — was lower than the 2.3% expected by Reuters-polled economists.
body: Core inflation in Japan soared to a fresh high in 2026, coming in at 2.2% in October as higher energy costs and their knock-on effects pushed up prices in the wider economy. Core inflation, which strips out prices of food, was lower than the 2.3% expected by Reuters-polled economists, but was higher than the 2.1% in prior month. Headline inflation came in at 2.3% compared with September's 2.1%, while the so-called "core-core" inflation, which strips out prices of fresh food and energy, dipped slightly to 2.2% from 2.4% in the month before, government data released on Friday showed. Energy subsidies for households expired in September, exposing consumers to higher prices brought about by the Iran war. Energy prices climbed 2.2% in October, a sharp spike from the 0.6% decline in September. Gas prices jumped 5.8% compared to the 2.4% rise the month before. Fuel, light and water charges also saw a considerable acceleration, increasing 3.4% compared to last month's 0.8%. Following the release, the Nikkei 225 index was down 2.1%, while the 10-year JGB yield fell 2 basis points to 2.805%. Japan has reportedly approved reintroduction of energy subsidies in December to stave off higher imported energy prices as higher prices crimp growth, hitting consumption and net exports. The October inflation reading is likely to push the Bank of Japan toward another rate hike in December, despite an unexpected contraction in economic growth in the third quarter. Data from LSEG indicates that there is a 72% chance of a 25 basis point hike from the Bank of Japan. On Wednesday, BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda told parliament that the central bank was also "mindful" of the weak yen and rising crude prices, saying that these could hurt ⁠households' real income and weigh on consumption more than expected. The yen marginally strengthened to trade at 159.59 against the dollar after the data release. Japan's inflation is likely to still stay above 2% for the rest of 2026 and into the first quarter of 2027, according to Ma Tieying, senior economist at DBS Group Research. She pointed out that while higher energy prices and yen weakness have contributed to headline inflation, the recent upturn is also supported by domestic factors. "Wage growth has remained above 3% for nine consecutive months, pointing to a broader pickup in underlying inflation as stronger wage gains feed through to services prices and household spending. This suggests a more durable wage–price cycle is taking hold." Ma expects the BOJ to raise rates in its December meeting, then twice more in 2027, bringing its terminal rate to 2%.

The developer of Claude nevertheless closed its first session 17% above the offer price, with a US$1.27tn market capitalisation. That is a powerful result for Anthropic as it raises capital to pursue AI growth, despite facing significant uncertainty as a result of it's very large future committed funding requirements and slowing revenue growth. Anthropic has the scale to explain the demand. Its filing records US$33.2bn of revenue in the nine months to September 2026, alongside a heavy operating loss. The company also cautions that its recent revenue growth may not continue at comparable rates. The spending commitments are just as important as the sales. Anthropic has committed to spending substantial sums under its Microsoft contract, regardless of actual usage. Its separate, conditional private placement is backed by Google, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and TSMC Partners. Those proposed investments sit alongside the public offer, rather than forming part of its proceeds. We think the lesson is selective capital, not a universal AI premium. Investors have backed a business with substantial revenue, but that revenue comes with formidable future costs. The market has priced in a very heavy premium on Anthropic, and with OpenAI potentially hitting the boards early next year, there is a question of where continued funding will come from. That could improve funding conditions for smaller software businesses as well as large AI developers. The recent fall in the price of Bitcoin may indicate a general rotation out of crypto into the AI trade. title: Anthropic IPO 'exactly what the markets need', but analysts warn of volatility - CNBC
body: Anthropic's blockbuster IPO on Thursday gave markets a much-needed boost after weeks of weakness, though analysts warned that the stock could remain volatile in the coming weeks. Share of the Claude maker opened at $111.50 and closed at $97.17 per share, 17% above the IPO price. The offering raised $81.3 billion through the sale of 980 million shares — surpassing SpaceX's June listing to become the largest IPO on record . Nomura strategist Charlie McElligott described investors as "foaming at the mouth" for the offering, with allocations "impossibly low," underscoring the strength of demand. "Anthropic's IPO is exactly what the markets need to revive overall sentiment," said Rebecca Walser, chief investment officer at Walser Wealth Management, adding that markets have been "depressed with all of the negativity in the AI complex over the past several weeks." While the initial pop was not surprising for such a highly anticipated listing, investors should avoid "chasing the IPO," Walser said. She expects the stock to come under pressure in the coming weeks as former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang testifies before the U.S. Senate , potentially reviving concerns around the AI sector. U.S. equities fell sharply on Thursday, with the tech heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.25% to end at 23,879.20, S&P 500 down 2.02% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average down 2.19%. Artificial intelligence and technology stocks initially rose thanks to the IPO, but the gains faded as "profit-taking spread across AI-related stocks," said Tiger Brokers chief market strategist James Ooi. "The shares remain highly volatile," said Morningstar senior equity analyst Malik Ahmed Khan. Walser said that any weakness around the testimony could offer an entry point for investors interested in Anthropic, adding that she remains bullish on the OpenAI rival over the long term. "For investors, it's going to become a blue-chip stock like Google," Ross Gerber, president and CEO of Gerber Kawasaki Wealth & Investment Management told CNBC. He added that U.S. technology valuations are at ridiculously low levels relative to the "crazy amazing innovation" coming out of California. Morningstar's Khan struck a more cautious tone, warning investors against getting swept up in the enthusiasm around Anthropic, advising them instead to step back and "carefully" assess the company as a long-term business. That will depend on Anthropic's ability to scale enterprise adoption, continue improving its models and turn those capabilities into economically useful products and services in the AI ecosystem, he said. "We remain confident that the firm will be able to execute on all three fronts," Khan added, setting a $92 fair value estimate for the stock. Walser stated that Anthropic is "extremely important for the overall AI story" as the first non-Chinese large language model developer to go public. Its listing gives public-market investors their first direct test of how a major standalone AI model developer will be valued and perform outside the chip sector. Meanwhile, rival OpenAI could follow with an IPO sometime in 2027. "This IPO is the show me moment for the AI story," Walser said, as much of the stock market's AI narrative has so far centered on chipmakers.

Senators voted 62-33 for the bill, with the majority of Republican Senators supporting the bill and getting joined by 14 Democrat Senators and one independent. The bill is now headed for the House. The new Democratic majority will not take office until January 2027, but those Democrats in the Senate who voted against it feared it would mean weaker environmental regulation, according to Reuters . “Tonight, the passage of permitting reform in the Senate finally became reality, and we took a major step towards addressing the affordability concerns of the American people,” Senator Shelley Moore Capito, co-author of the bill, said following the vote. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Bill got broad support from the Senate before the midterms, but voting on it was scheduled for after the elections. It was meant to speed up permitting for new energy projects, including both oil, gas, and coal projects, and alternative energy installations such as wind and solar. Many Democrats in Congress worry about the bill affecting earlier environmental regulations and weakening net-zero stipulations in earlier legislation. “Embedded in this bill is a fundamental question about the direction we go regarding our responsibilities to this planet,” Senator Jeff Merkley of Oregon commented ahead of the vote, as quoted by CBS News. Merkley acknowledged that the bill could, in fact, “turn the faucet potentially on” for wind and solar projects but suspected the Trump administration would just block these in favor of hydrocarbons. Given that President Trump has already dismantled as much of pro-transition legislation as he could, these fears may be a bit surplus at this time. summary: The PPI for October came in at 5.7%, compared to the 5.3% expected by economists polled by Reuters.
body: Producer prices in China grew at the fastest rate since June 2022, accelerating for the third month in a row. The PPI for October came in at 5.7%, compared to the 5.3% expected by economists polled by Reuters. The increase was driven by a sharp rise in prices in the mining and raw materials industries. The increase was driven by very strong external demand, Zhang Zhiwei, president and chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management, told CNBC's " Squawk Box Asia ." Consumer inflation in China slowed to 0.7% in October, its first deceleration after two straight months of increases. The figure missed expectations of a 0.8% rise from economists polled by Reuters, and was lower than the 0.9% seen in September. Core inflation, which strips out food and energy prices, came in at 0.8%, down from the 1% seen in the month before. The rise in consumer prices were still held up by prices of gasoline, which was the largest contributor to the increase in prices, but this was offset by a sharper than expected fall in food prices, according to Dong Lijuan, chief statistician of the urban division at China's National Bureau of Statistics. The Chinese economy has shown some signs of expansion recently. It grew faster than expected in the third quarter, and September saw a sharp beat in retail sales. The mainland Chinese CSI 300 index gained 0.56% after the data release. Pinpoint's Zhang said that domestic demand has been rather weak due to the property market, and this is a key reason why inflation is not picking up in China "There's no clear sign of stabilization [in that sector] yet," he said, adding this was weighing on the household consumer confidence and local government revenue. "So the the overall economic momentum has been weak and hasn't really seen [a] clear sign of recovery," Zhang explained.

body: NVIDIA’s NVDA Q3 fiscal year 2027 (FY2027) earnings report , guidance, and conference call mark a turning point for AI investors. While fears and risks remain, the Huang Affair effectively ended AI’s speculation phase, and the Q3 results point to the next phase: execution. Execution means converting massive backlogs into cash flow, turning plans into data centers, and capitalizing on investments that, for NVIDIA, span its ecosystem and future revenue paths. The primary takeaway from the release is momentum. NVIDIA’s results reflect momentum, as do the guidance and longer-term forecasts. As interim CEO Colette Kress pointed out, the long-term 2028 guidance is higher than the prior forecast on a larger base, representing a massive increase in the forward outlook sufficient to validate signals from other AI-critical companies. Oracle ORCL , Micron MU , Astera Labs ALAB , and Credo Technologies CRDO are just a few companies indicating strength, with guidance forecasting acceleration over the next few quarters. More importantly, these companies are inflecting or on track to reach positive cash flow and profitability, perhaps the single most important factor for investors. NVIDIA Signals Multi-Year Roadmap Intact: Vera Rubin Sales Are Ramping NVIDIA’s Q3 results continued the trend, outperforming MarketBeat’s consensus estimates by several percentage points on strength in Data Centers and AI. The Data Center business led, growing more than 100% year over year (YOY), but it isn’t the only strength, as Edge Computing also posted solid growth of about 42%. Within this, Vera Rubin added nearly $20 billion in sequential revenue, representing the fastest product ramp in company history (since Blackwell). As strong as the revenue is, margins and guidance are the market triggers. Margins improved, driving ample cash flow and balance sheet improvements to backstop NVIDIA’s investment and spending commitments. Guidance, including management commentary, reflects a steady, stable market in which customers remain committed to product cycles, with Q4 FY2027 revenue expected to grow nearly 91% YOY, ahead of consensus expectations, in addition to Q3 strength. Further out, Kress and team expect approximately 75% growth in fiscal 2028, up 5 percentage points from the prior forecast. Board Signals Confidence, Shifting Focus With Buyback Authorization Buyback plans are a signal for investors to watch, and they are strengthening along with the business. The board authorized an additional $150 billion in September, bringing the total available funds to over $225 billion, a sign of confidence in the cash flow. The $225 billion is a relatively small amount compared with NVIDIA’s market cap but sufficient to reduce the share count, and more repurchases are expected. Execs remain committed to focusing free cash flow on capital returns, net of investments, which some analysts forecast to slow. Speculation is that the company will slow its aggressive investment cycle, having secured its multi-year growth trajectory, and shift cash flow to capital returns, specifically buybacks. Balance sheet and cash flow highlights support the thesis that buybacks will accelerate; cash is up nearly 3x year-to-date, and investments, receivables, inventory, current, and total assets are up, outpacing liabilities and driving equity, despite the business investments. Liabilities remain low relative to equity and cash flow, and cash flow is forecast to improve sequentially in fiscal 2028. Q3 operating cash flow topped $48 billion, leaving more than $43 billion in free cash flow after capital spending. Quarterly returns topped $28 billion, up more than 120% year over year, leaving ample cushion for future increases. Initial analyst responses reflect cautious optimism and reinforce NVDA's upside potential.
